How belonging changes the way students read ambiguous feedback

experiment
preregistration
replication
survey design
Qualtrics
R
Three studies, one preregistered replication, N = 1,125: students who feel they belong read the same ambiguous comment more charitably, and gender shapes which feedback format they prefer.
Published

January 15, 2025

In brief. Academic feedback is often ambiguous (“interesting approach”), and what a student does with it depends on how they read it. Across an exploratory study (n = 423), a preregistered direct replication with a power analysis and a preregistered effect-size range for success (n = 233), and a preregistered extension (n = 469), lower social belonging predicted more negative evaluation of the same feedback, and the replication landed inside its preregistered range. Published in Social Psychology of Education (2025).

N = 1,125exploratory → confirmatorypower analysispreregistered replication rangeQualtrics

Why this mattered

Feedback is the cheapest intervention in education and one of the least understood. If two students read the same sentence differently because of how much they feel they belong, then feedback quality is not a property of the sentence alone, and improving it means attending to the reader.

What I did

Study 1 was exploratory and generated the hypotheses. Study 2 was a direct replication with preregistered confirmatory hypotheses, a power analysis based on Study 1, exclusion rules fixed in advance, and a preregistered criterion for what would count as a successful replication (an R² range). Study 3 was a preregistered conceptual replication and extension that moved the outcome from forced choice to Likert-type scales. All three ran on Qualtrics with a university participant pool.

What I found

Lower belonging predicted more negative evaluation of ambiguous feedback in all three studies. The Study 2 model landed inside the preregistered replication range. Gender differences appeared in feedback-format preferences.

What a team would do with this

This is the study I point to when someone asks how I decide that evidence is sufficient. The answer is written down before the data arrive: the hypothesis, the sample size, the exclusions, and the range of effects that will count. That discipline transfers directly to A/B testing and to any program where the temptation is to read a result after the fact.
